items.answer: The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is a widely used questionnaire for measuring cybersickness in immersive experiences. It contains 16 items in oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales, rated from 0 to 3, with subscale and total sickness scores.
A questionnaire is a set of questions or statements provided to users to rate in user evaluation, although it need not contain questions.
A seven-point rating scale is a rating scale for statements that ranges from 1 to 7, with 1 indicating strong disagreement and 7 indicating strong agreement.
A statistically significant difference is an observed difference in data that a statistical significance test indicates is not due to chance.

Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

questions.question: What was the central aim of the Majuli VR tour?
options: To preserve disappearing heritage through an immersive experience
To evaluate head-mounted displays through an immersive experience
To measure cyber sickness through an immersive experience
To teach controller navigation through an immersive experience
questions.explanation: The Majuli VR tour was intended to capture and digitally preserve the island’s ecological and cultural heritage because the island is disappearing. Evaluating hardware, teaching navigation, or measuring cybersickness are not the tour’s central aim.

questions.question: Which three usability outcomes did the Majuli VR tour evaluation intend to measure?
options: Frame latency, head tracking, and display resolution
Tangible accuracy, cultural accuracy, and immersion duration
User engagement, presence, and comfort
Navigation time, path length, and task completion
questions.explanation: The evaluation was aimed at usability in the virtual environment, specifically user engagement, presence, and comfort. Hardware metrics, navigation-efficiency measures, and heritage-accuracy judgments are different kinds of outcomes.

questions.question: Besides a controlled experiment, what other method did the Majuli VR tour evaluation use to collect end-user data?
options: A field deployment
A participant interview
A performance benchmark
A structured questionnaire
questions.explanation: The evaluation combined a controlled experiment with a structured questionnaire, while interviews, field deployments, and benchmarks were not the collection methods.

data.text: The Majuli VR tour case study has a heritage-preservation purpose and a defined evaluation method. The tour aims to digitally preserve the island's tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage because the island is disappearing. Its evaluation focuses on usability, including engagement, presence, comfort, and cyber sickness symptoms, to identify improvements. Data come from a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire connected to the research question, using subjective, objective, behavioral, or rating-scale responses.
points: The Majuli VR tour digitally preserves Majuli's tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage because the island is disappearing.
The Majuli VR tour evaluation measures usability, engagement, presence, comfort, and cyber sickness symptoms to identify improvements.
The Majuli VR tour evaluation collected end-user data subjectively, objectively, or both via controlled experiment and structured questionnaire.
The Majuli VR tour's structured questionnaire related to the evaluation research question and could measure objective, behavioral, or rating-scale data.

questions.question: Why were the 27 Majuli VR tour participants divided into three groups of nine?
options: To cover the full age range of the participants
To balance the male and female numbers
To represent the tour system's supported user categories
To compare different levels of prior virtual reality experience
questions.explanation: The groups corresponded to the user categories supported by the tour system, with participants selected to match those categories. Sex balance, VR experience level, and age coverage were not the grouping rationale.

questions.question: Why is prior virtual reality experience noted for 21 participants in the Majuli VR tour study?
options: It may reduce the measured comfort
It may speed the measured navigation
It may bias the measured results
It may lower the measured sickness
questions.explanation: Prior virtual reality experience can bias the measured results because experienced participants may respond differently. It is not stated that it reduces comfort, speeds navigation, or lowers sickness.

questions.question: How were participants positioned while performing the tasks in the Majuli VR tour evaluation?
options: They were standing on a fixed platform
They were seated on a swivel chair
They were lying on a reclined bench
They were walking on an open floor
questions.explanation: Participants sat on a swivel chair during the tasks. Standing, lying, and walking positions are not part of the described setup.

questions.question: What prior interaction ability did every participant in the Majuli VR tour evaluation have?
options: Familiarity with a keyboard and mouse and menu-based interaction
Familiarity with a handheld motion-tracking controller and gesture-based interaction
Familiarity with a joystick-based controller and controller-based interaction
Familiarity with a gamepad controller and button-based interaction
questions.explanation: All participants had used the joystick-based controller and controller-based interaction in a virtual or non-virtual context. The other options name different input forms rather than the prior ability established for the study.

data.text: The evaluation setup for the Majuli VR tour describes the volunteer pool and the platform that presented the tour. The volunteers represent pilgrims, students, and tourists, with most having prior VR experience and all familiar with the joystick controller and having normal or corrected-to-normal vision. The standard Meta Quest 2 platform was connected to a Windows 11 PC through Oculus Link, and participants performed tasks seated.
points: The Majuli VR tour evaluation used 27 volunteers aged 23-40, mean 25.1, in pilgrim, student, and tourist groups.
Most Majuli VR tour participants had prior VR experience, which may bias evaluation output.
All Majuli VR tour participants were familiar with the joystick controller and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
The standard setup linked the Meta Quest 2 via Oculus Link to a Windows 11 PC with a GTX 1080.
During tasks, Majuli VR tour participants were seated on a swivel chair.

questions.question: In the Majuli VR tour evaluation, what type of standard instrument is the QEP?
options: A revised standard sickness questionnaire
A revised standard presence questionnaire
A revised standard familiarity questionnaire
A revised standard comfort questionnaire
questions.explanation: The QEP is a revised version of a standard presence questionnaire, so it is used to measure presence. It is not a sickness, comfort, or familiarity questionnaire.

questions.question: What personal comparison did the added QEP items ask participants to make about the Majuli VR tour?
options: Whether they had previously visited the island and whether the tour matched that real experience
Whether they had previously used a VR headset and whether the tour matched that earlier experience
Whether they had previously read about the island and whether the tour matched that written experience
Whether they had previously seen images of the island and whether the tour matched that visual experience
questions.explanation: The tailored QEP items asked whether participants had previously visited the island in person and whether the virtual tour corresponded with their real visit. Earlier headset use, images, or reading are not the comparisons asked.

questions.question: What purpose did the pre- and post-session simulator sickness questionnaire scores serve in the Majuli VR tour evaluation?
options: To compare the change in familiarity and infer the tour design's effect
To compare the change in those scores and infer the tour design's effect
To compare the change in comfort and infer the tour design's effect
To compare the change in presence and infer the tour design's effect
questions.explanation: The SSQ scores were computed before and after exposure so that the change in sickness scores could be compared and the effect of the tour design could be assessed. Presence, comfort, and familiarity were not the scores being compared for that purpose.

questions.question: What is notable about the simulator sickness questionnaire's role in immersive-experience evaluation?
options: It is widely used for familiarity although it was not developed for that purpose
It is widely used for presence although it was not developed for that purpose
It is widely used for comfort although it was not developed for that purpose
It is widely used for cyber sickness although it was not developed for that purpose
questions.explanation: The SSQ is popular for measuring cyber sickness in immersive experiences, but it was not originally developed for that purpose. It is not a presence, comfort, or familiarity measure.

data.text: Presence and cyber sickness in the Majuli VR tour evaluation are measured with established questionnaires and rating scales. Presence uses the QEP, a revised presence questionnaire with 19 core and 3 optional sound items rated 1 to 7, plus two Majuli visit items; cyber sickness uses the SSQ, rated 0 to 3, with nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness compared before and after exposure.
points: Presence is measured with the QEP questionnaire, a 2004 revision of the standard presence questionnaire.
The QEP has 19 core and 3 optional sound items, with responses on a 1-to-7 Likert scale.
The QEP added two Majuli VR items about prior in-person visits and whether the tour matched them.
Cyber sickness is measured with the standard SSQ, though not originally for it, using 0 no symptoms to 3 severe.
The SSQ scores considered were nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness, compared before and after exposure.

questions.question: Why is a short session that shows a VR system's features and controls given to participants before an experiment?
options: To reduce presence-related bias by teaching participants how to report their presence ratings before the experiment
To reduce familiarity or prior-experience bias by bringing participants to a similar level before the experiment
To reduce sickness-related bias by giving participants a mild exposure to the system before the experiment
To reduce realism-related bias by explaining what a virtual environment is before the experiment
questions.explanation: A brief training session is used to level participants' familiarity with the system, reducing prior-experience bias that could otherwise distort the results. It is not a sickness exposure, presence-rating lesson, or realism explanation.

questions.question: Why does the VR tour evaluation include a pre-exposure assessment and a post-exposure assessment?
options: To detect change in heritage understanding across the experimental session
To detect change in presence across the experimental session
To detect change in system familiarity across the experimental session
To detect change in cybersickness across the experimental session
questions.explanation: The pre-exposure and post-exposure measures are the simulator sickness questionnaire, so they let researchers see whether cybersickness changes during the VR session. Presence is measured only after exploration, so a pre/post presence comparison is not supported.

questions.question: What trade-off guided the choice of the fixed session length in the VR tour evaluation?
options: Enough time for questionnaires and interviews, while limiting sickness exposure
Enough time for device and software setup, while limiting sickness exposure
Enough time for the large island and heritage content, while limiting sickness exposure
Enough time for real-visit comparison, while limiting sickness exposure
questions.explanation: The session length balanced sufficient time to cover the large island and heritage information against the risk that longer exposure increases cybersickness. It was not chosen primarily for questionnaires, real-visit comparison, or equipment setup.

questions.question: In a standard controlled experiment, what is the main purpose of defining the procedure?
options: To prepare the hardware, software, and questionnaires in the experiment
To eliminate possible biases in the experiment
To define the users and identify participants in the experiment
To demonstrate the system's features and controls in the experiment
questions.explanation: Defining the procedure is the stage where the experiment is arranged to reduce or remove bias. Preparing setup and identifying participants are separate stages, and demonstrating system features is a specific training activity rather than the main purpose of the procedure.

data.text: The controlled VR tour evaluation follows standard experimental stages: defining and identifying users, preparing hardware, software, questionnaires and logistics, and setting a bias-eliminating procedure. Brief pre-experiment training helps make unfamiliar users comparable with familiar users by reducing prior-experience bias. Participants then complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exposure and the presence questionnaire after exploration. Finally, each participant individually explores the whole tour for 45 to 50 minutes, a time estimated to provide heritage access while limiting exposure-linked cybersickness.
points: A controlled experiment defines users, identifies participants, prepares hardware, software, questionnaires and logistics, with a procedure that eliminates bias.
Brief pre-experiment training can equalize users by demonstrating the VR system's features and use, reducing familiarity or prior-experience bias.
Participants complete the simulator sickness questionnaire before and after exposure and the presence questionnaire after VR exploration.
The 45 to 50 minute individual, controlled VR tour exploration was estimated to allow heritage access and limit exposure-linked cybersickness.

questions.question: Which participant group received additional tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity ratings in the Majuli virtual tour evaluation?
options: Participants who had explored the tour in a controlled setting
Participants who had previously used digital tour systems
Participants who had previously visited Majuli Island
Participants who had completed the post-exposure sickness questionnaire
questions.explanation: The additional tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity ratings were reported for the participants who had previously visited the island. Prior use of digital tours or completion of the sickness questionnaire does not identify that group.

questions.question: What did the overall good presence rating for the Majuli virtual tour indicate about users' experience?
options: They reported that the tour made cybersickness symptoms disappear during exploration
They felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while exploring the island
They felt completely transported to the physical island and lost awareness of the interface
They concluded that the virtual island was visually indistinguishable from the physical island
questions.explanation: Good presence meant that users felt reasonably well located inside the virtual environment while exploring Majuli. It did not claim complete indistinguishability from the real island, nor was it a statement about cybersickness.

questions.question: What did previous visitors' more favorable presence ratings, given their higher expectations, indicate about the Majuli virtual tour?
options: They indicated that the tour's visual quality was the main factor behind the more favorable ratings
They indicated that the tour reasonably matched the physical island in its design, interaction, and implementation
They indicated that previous visitors needed less realistic interaction and a simpler interface than first-time visitors
They indicated that the digital avatar was less important to the overall presence experience than the interface
questions.explanation: Previous visitors' more favorable ratings showed that the system reasonably mimicked the physical island in its design elements, interaction, and overall implementation. The result is not an attribution mainly to visual quality, a simpler interface, or the relative importance of the avatar.

questions.question: What did the statistically significant Welch t-test result support in the Majuli virtual tour evaluation?
options: It supported the conclusion that prior exposure to digital or virtual tours helped users gain a better experience
It supported the conclusion that prior exposure to digital or virtual tours improved the interface rating more than the immersion rating
It supported the conclusion that prior exposure to digital or virtual tours reduced cybersickness during the tour
It supported the conclusion that unfamiliar users produced the same presence ratings as familiar users
questions.explanation: The Welch t-test showed a statistically significant difference between users with and without prior exposure to digital or virtual tours, supporting that prior exposure helped users gain a better experience. It did not establish a cybersickness effect, a specific interface advantage, or equal ratings between familiar and unfamiliar users.

data.text: The presence evaluation of the Majuli VR tour used involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, visual fidelity, and reconstruction fidelity for previous visitors. The overall ratings indicate good presence, while previous visitors' more favorable ratings suggest the tour's design and avatar closely matched the physical island. A significant difference between users with and without prior exposure supported the conclusion that such exposure always helps users gain a better experience.
points: Majuli VR tour presence measures included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, visual fidelity, and reconstruction fidelity for previous visitors.
Overall Majuli VR tour presence was good, meaning users felt reasonably well located while virtually exploring.
Previous visitors' more favorable ratings showed the tour reasonably mimicked the physical island and its avatar was close to reality.
A Welch t-test showed a significant difference, supporting that prior digital or virtual tour exposure always helps.

questions.question: Which pre- and post-exposure SSQ items were found to differ significantly in the Majuli VR tour evaluation?
options: Disorientation and oculomotor SSQ items
Nausea and total SSQ items
Oculomotor and total SSQ items
Nausea and disorientation SSQ items
questions.explanation: The pre- and post-exposure comparison found significant changes for the oculomotor and total sickness items, not for nausea or disorientation.

questions.question: What conclusion follows from the small pre- and post-exposure differences in nausea and disorientation for the Majuli VR tour?
options: The tour showed a disorientation-driven sickness effect
The tour showed no general sickness effect
The tour showed an oculomotor-driven sickness effect
The tour showed a nausea-driven sickness effect
questions.explanation: Little change in nausea and disorientation indicates that the tour did not generally induce cybersickness, although some other sickness measures still changed.

questions.question: What does a statistically significant pre- and post-exposure change in total sickness indicate about the Majuli VR tour?
options: A prior-exposure effect on total sickness
A latency effect on total sickness
A design effect on total sickness
An age effect on total sickness
questions.explanation: The significant change in total sickness is interpreted as showing that the tour design had some effect on total sickness, not specifically as a latency, age, or prior-exposure effect.

data.text: The Majuli VR tour cyber sickness evaluation compared pre- and post-exposure SSQ scores for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor, and total severity. The results showed little change in nausea and disorientation, so the tour did not generally induce cyber sickness, while the oculomotor and total sickness outcomes changed. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test then showed those oculomotor and total sickness changes were statistically significant, indicating the tour design had some effect on total sickness.
points: The Majuli VR tour cyber sickness evaluation collected pre- and post-exposure SSQ scores for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor, and total severity.
Majuli VR tour evaluation showed little nausea and disorientation change, suggesting it did not generally induce cyber sickness.
A Wilcoxon signed-rank test found statistically significant pre-to-post changes for oculomotor and total sickness, showing the design affected total sickness.

questions.question: How might a user's prior experience influence their reaction to the Majuli virtual tour?
options: More unfamiliar
Less acceptable
More acceptable
More disorienting
questions.explanation: Prior experience may lead to better results, with experienced users possibly finding the tour more acceptable. There is no basis for saying that prior experience makes the tour less acceptable, more disorienting, or more unfamiliar.

questions.question: Which cybersickness component could explain a possible change in total sickness for the Majuli virtual tour?
options: The oculomotor component
The nausea component
The total sickness component
The disorientation component
questions.explanation: The oculomotor component may have been affected, and that effect could contribute to a change in total sickness. Nausea and disorientation did not show a clear severity effect, while total sickness is the overall score rather than an explanatory component.

data.text: The evaluation of the Majuli VR Tour reports presence and cybersickness outcomes. The presence result is generally positive, and experienced users may find the tour more acceptable. The cybersickness finding is more limited: certain items were not found to affect severity, but the oculomotor component may still influence total sickness.
points: The Majuli VR Tour's presence results were mostly good, and experienced users may find it more acceptable than inexperienced users.
Some Majuli VR Tour cybersickness items were not found to affect severity, but the oculomotor component may influence total sickness.

questions.question: What does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test result tell us about the cybersickness changes observed in the Majuli virtual reality tour evaluation?
questions.reference_answer: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that the pre- and post-exposure differences for the oculomotor item and total sickness were not due to chance. Thus, although box plots showed little change in nausea and disorientation and the tour did not generally induce cybersickness, the tour design had some effect on total sickness.

questions.question: How does the additional reconstruction-fidelity rating for previous visitors help interpret the presence results for the Majuli virtual reality tour?
questions.reference_answer: The questionnaire for environmental presence was tailored with items asking previous visitors whether the virtual tour matched their real visit. Their ratings were more favorable on all presence factors, including tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity. This suggests that the tour's design elements, interaction, implementation and digital avatar reasonably mimicked the physical island, even with higher expectations.

questions.question: Why was the Majuli virtual reality tour exploration limited to about 45 to 50 minutes?
questions.reference_answer: The 45 to 50 minute exploration time was estimated from pilot studies, trials, and literature to give users sufficient time to explore the large island and obtain heritage information. It was also chosen to minimize the possibility of cybersickness, which depends on exposure.
